title: Obadiah

stories.title: 🦅 Obadiah
summaryBullets: This is the vision of Obadiah: This is what the Lord GOD says about Edom — We have heard a message from the LORD; an envoy has been sent among the nations to say, “Rise up, and let us go to battle against her!”— (1:1).
“Behold, I will make you small among the nations; you will be deeply despised. (1:2).
The pride of your heart has deceived you, O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks whose habitation is the heights, who say in your heart, ‘Who can bring me down to the ground?’ (1:3).
Though you soar like the eagle and make your nest among the stars, even from there I will bring you down,” declares the LORD. (1:4).
“If thieves came to you, if robbers by night — oh, how you will be ruined — would they not steal only what they wanted? If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave some gleanings? (1:5).
But how Esau will be pillaged, his hidden treasures sought out! (1:6).

All the men allied with you will drive you to the border; the men at peace with you will deceive and overpower you. Those who eat your bread will set a trap for you without your awareness of it. (1:7).
In that day, declares the LORD, will I not destroy the wise men of Edom and the men of understanding in the mountains of Esau? (1:8).
Then your mighty men, O Teman, will be terrified, so that everyone in the mountains of Esau will be cut down in the slaughter. (1:9).
Because of the violence against your brother Jacob, you will be covered with shame and cut off forever. (1:10).
On the day you stood aloof while strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gate and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were just like one of them. (1:11).
But you should not gloat in that day, your brother’s day of misfortune, nor rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their destruction, nor boast proudly in the day of their distress. (1:12).
You should not enter the gate of My people in the day of their disaster, nor gloat over their affliction in the day of their disaster, nor loot their wealth in the day of their disaster. (1:13).
Nor should you stand at the crossroads to cut off their fugitives, nor deliver up their survivors in the day of their distress. (1:14).
For the Day of the LORD is near for all the nations. As you have done, it will be done to you; your recompense will return upon your own head. (1:15).
For as you drank on My holy mountain, so all the nations will drink continually. They will drink and gulp it down; they will be as if they had never existed. (1:16).
But on Mount Zion there will be deliverance, and it will be holy, and the house of Jacob will reclaim their possession. (1:17).

Then the house of Jacob will be a blazing fire, and the house of Joseph a burning flame; but the house of Esau will be stubble — Jacob will set it ablaze and consume it. Therefore no survivor will remain from the house of Esau.” For the LORD has spoken. (1:18).

Those from the Negev will possess the mountains of Esau; those from the foothills will possess the land of the Philistines. They will occupy the fields of Ephraim and Samaria, and Benjamin will possess Gilead. (1:19).

And the exiles of this host of the Israelites will possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath; and the exiles from Jerusalem who are in Sepharad will possess the cities of the Negev. (1:20).
The deliverers will ascend Mount Zion to rule over the mountains of Esau. And the kingdom will belong to the LORD. (1:21).
crossRefs: Numbers 20:14-21: Edom’s refusal to Israel (hostility roots).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֱדוֹם (ʾEdom), עֵשָׂו (ʿEsav), שֵׂעִיר (Seʿir), Greek (LXX): Ἐδώμ, Ἠσαῦ, Σηείρ, Aramaic: אדום, עשו, שעיר
translationNotes.note: People/land descended from Esau dwelling in Mount Seir (the rugged highlands south of Judah).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צִיר (tsir, ‘envoy/messenger’), Greek (LXX): ἄγγελος, Aramaic: שליחא (shliḥa)
translationNotes.note: The report/mission that calls nations against Edom (1:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַגְוֵי־סֶלַע (ḥagvê-selaʿ), Greek (LXX): τὰς ὀπὰς τοῦ πέτρας, Aramaic: נקיקי טורא
translationNotes.note: High rock dwellings (cf. Sela/Petra) Edom trusted for safety (1:3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶשֶׁר (nesher), Greek (LXX): ἀετός, Aramaic: נשרא
translationNotes.note: Image of height/speed; even there God says He will bring Edom down (1:4).

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

stories.keyTakeaway: God declares judgment on Edom’s arrogant security in its rock strongholds; He Himself will bring them down.

intro:
Obadiah was written by Obadiah (Obadiah 1:1), of whom no patronymic or village is recorded; the prophet is identified only by name. The book is the shortest in the Old Testament, twenty-one verses comprising a single chapter, and consists of one extended oracle against the kingdom of Edom. The date of composition is debated within Bible-affirming tradition between two main views. The early view places the book in the ninth century BC, during the reign of King Jehoram of Judah (848-841 BC), when Edom rebelled against Judah and a coalition of Philistines and Arabs from the south invaded Jerusalem and looted the royal palace (2 Kings 8:20-22; 2 Chronicles 21:8-17); this view connects to the Jewish tradition (preserved in the Talmud, Sanhedrin 39b) that identifies the prophet Obadiah with Obadiah the steward of Ahab's household who hid one hundred prophets from Queen Jezebel (1 Kings 18:3-16). The later view places the book shortly after the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar II in 586 BC, when the Edomites assisted the Babylonians, cheered the destruction, captured fugitives, and looted the city (events also condemned in Psalm 137:7, Lamentations 4:21-22, Ezekiel 25:12-14, and Ezekiel 35:1-15). The prophet's name Ovadyah (עֹבַדְיָה) is a common Hebrew name meaning "servant of Yahuah" or "worshipper of Yahuah," combining the noun eved ("servant") with the divine name Yah. At least a dozen other Obadiahs appear in the Old Testament, including Obadiah the steward of King Ahab (1 Kings 18:3-16, the candidate of the early-date tradition), an Issacharite warrior chief (1 Chronicles 7:3), a chief musician of the Levites (1 Chronicles 9:16), a leader of returning exiles under Ezra (Ezra 8:9), and a covenant signatory under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:5); none are identical with the prophet of this book under either dating view.

The historical setting in both proposed dates is the recurring conflict between Edom and Judah. The Edomites were descendants of Esau, the elder brother of Jacob (Genesis 25:23-26; 36:8-9, "Esau is Edom"). Edom occupied the rugged mountain country southeast of the Dead Sea, with its capital later at the cliff-cut city of Sela (the later Nabataean Petra). Edomites and Israelites had hostile relations from the Exodus onward: Moses had requested passage through Edom and been refused (Numbers 20:14-21); Saul, David, and the later kings fought repeated wars against them. Obadiah verses 11-14's vivid description of Edom standing aloof while strangers entered Jerusalem's gates, casting lots over its wealth, and seizing fugitives at the crossroads fits the experience of either the ninth-century invasion or the sixth-century destruction. After the Babylonian period, Edom was eventually overrun by Nabataean Arabs migrating from the east; the displaced Edomites moved into southern Judah (Idumea in Greek) and were eventually forcibly converted to Judaism by the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus around 125 BC. Herod the Great, the Idumean king who ruled Judea at the time of Jesus' birth, was a descendant of these converted Edomites.

Obadiah is the thirty-first book of the Christian Old Testament and the fourth of the twelve Minor Prophets, the shortest book in the Old Testament. The Hebrew name Ovadyah (עֹבַדְיָה) is the prophet's own name. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Obadiah were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), preserved as part of the Twelve Minor Prophets scrolls; the earliest copies date to the 2nd century BC. The opening of Obadiah's oracle (verses 1-9) closely parallels Jeremiah 49:7-22, both prophets sharing material in their oracles against Edom; under either dating of Obadiah, the two prophets drew on the same prophetic source, with traditional views holding that Jeremiah quoted Obadiah (early-date view) or that both prophets received similar oracles (late-date view).
